# The workflow in a nutshell

**WolfPackR** puts genotyped individuals into packs by combining who is related to whom (genetics) with who uses which space (non-invasive samples: scats, urine, hair...). The typical workflow has four steps:

1. `genetic_groups()`: families, from pairwise relatedness (e.g. computed by `relatedness()`), found by community detection (Leiden by default);
2. `space_use()`: the space use of every individual, as a kernel density (utilisation distribution, UD) on a common grid, with one bandwidth `h` for everybody, so that individuals with a single sample are handled like the others;
3. `assign_individuals()`: each family gets a reference territory, each sample goes to the territory it falls in (or "outside"), each individual goes where most of its samples are, and gets a status (Resident, Putative disperser, Disperser, Unrelated resident, Transient, Undetermined);
4. `spatial_groups()`: families spread over several territories are split into spatially coherent packs.

Then `summarise_packs()`, `plot_packs()` and `pack_timeline()` describe the packs, and `compare_partitions()` and `pack_stability()` check how good and how robust they are. `wolf_packs()` runs steps 1 to 4 in one go.

```{r load}
library(WolfPackR)
```

---

# A quick run on simulated data

Nine fictitious wolves, with Wang's relatedness:

```{r toy}
data("samples_example")
data("relate_example")
toy <- wolf_packs(samples_example, relate_example, estimator = "wang", threshold = 0.4)
toy
toy$individuals[, c("Individual", "Genetic_Group", "Pack", "Status", "split")]
plot_packs(toy$samples, "Pack", ud = toy$ud)
```

---

# Step by step: wolves of the Romanian Carpathians

263 non-invasive genetic samples of 47 wolves (one of them a wolf x dog hybrid) collected from 2017 to 2020 (Foundation Conservation Carpathia, 2024; Iosif et al., 2025), with their 22-microsatellite genotypes.

```{r carpat-data}
data("samples_Carpathians")
data("genotypes_Carpathians")
table(samples_Carpathians$Campaign)
```

## 1. Relatedness and genetic groups

Relatedness is computed from the genotypes, leaving the hybrid out of the allele frequencies. With the Queller & Goodnight estimator, 0.25 is the value expected for second-degree relatives (0.5 for first-degree ones). A few spurious links are unavoidable at this threshold: community detection (Leiden) keeps them from chaining families together, which connected components would do. The null model compares the modularity of the groups with that of random graphs.

```{r genetic}
rel <- relatedness(genotypes_Carpathians,
                   freq_ids = setdiff(genotypes_Carpathians$Individual, "EF.15J8"))
gen <- genetic_groups(rel, estimator = "QG", threshold = 0.25, n_null = 99)
attr(gen, "modularity")
table(table(gen$group))          # group sizes
```

## 2. Space use

```{r space}
obs <- merge(samples_Carpathians, gen, by = "Individual")
ud <- space_use(obs)             # bandwidth chosen from the well-sampled individuals
ud
round(ud_overlap(ud)[1:5, 1:5], 2)
```

## 3. Assigning individuals

With the relatedness table, relatives are defined pair by pair. With `period`, the spread of each individual is measured within each sampling season, and dispersal can be dated.

```{r assign}
ai <- assign_individuals(obs, "group", ud = ud, relate = rel, estimator = "QG", threshold = 0.25,
                         period = "Campaign")
table(ai$Status)
ai[ai$Status != "Resident", c("Individual", "Genetic_Group", "Group", "Status", "n_samples", "split")]
```

## 4. Spatially coherent packs

```{r packs}
obs$Group <- ai$Group[match(obs$Individual, ai$Individual)]
packs <- spatial_groups(obs, "Group", ud = ud, period = "Campaign")
table(packs$Pack, useNA = "ifany")
```

## Describing the packs

```{r describe}
obs$Pack <- packs$Pack[match(obs$Individual, packs$Individual)]
obs$Status <- ai$Status[match(obs$Individual, ai$Individual)]
summarise_packs(obs, "Pack", ud = ud, relate = rel, estimator = "QG", n_perm = 199)
plot_packs(obs, "Pack", ud = ud)
```

`shared_pct` is the share of each territory (95% isopleth) that lies inside the territory of another pack, and `nearest_km` the distance to the nearest pack.

## Through time

`pack_timeline()` follows each individual and each territory from one season to the next: who was detected in which territory, who changed pack, and how far each territory moved.

```{r timeline}
tl <- pack_timeline(obs, "Pack", period = "Campaign", ud = ud)
table(tl$individuals$pattern)
tl$individuals[tl$individuals$pattern == "changed pack", 1:7]
tl$territories
```

With `period` and `date`, `summarise_packs()` sums this up for each pack, following the land tenure framework of Kanishka et al. (2026): seasons in which the pack was detected in its territory, members detected there in more than one season, lowest affinity between a seasonal territory and the territory over all seasons, largest shift, and time from the first to the last detection.

```{r tenure}
sm <- summarise_packs(obs, "Pack", ud = ud, period = "Campaign", date = "Date")
sm[, c("Pack", "first_period", "last_period", "n_periods", "n_persistent", "min_affinity", "max_shift_km", "tenure_years")]
```

These are minimum values that depend on the sampling: a pack missing from a season may not have been sampled there (a single sample was collected in the territory of pack 4 in 2017-18, see `effort_Carpathians`), seasonal territories drawn from few samples are smaller, and a 3-season study can't measure tenures longer than itself.

---

# All at once, and how good it is

`wolf_packs()` runs the four steps with the same settings:

```{r all}
res <- wolf_packs(samples_Carpathians, rel, "QG", 0.25, period = "Campaign")
res
```

The packs of Iosif et al. (2025), reconstructed from parentage, serve as a reference:

```{r validation}
data("reference_Carpathians")
compare_partitions(res$individuals, reference_Carpathians)
```

And how much do the packs depend on the settings and on sampling chance?

```{r stability}
st <- pack_stability(samples_Carpathians, rel, "QG", 0.25,
                     vary = list(threshold = c(0.2, 0.25, 0.3), h = c(1500, 2500)),
                     n_boot = 10, reference = reference_Carpathians, period = "Campaign")
st$runs
head(st$individuals[order(st$individuals$stability), ])
```

Is the sampling dense enough? Subsampling keeps only part of the samples, as with a lighter field effort, and shows how fast the packs degrade:

```{r subsampling}
sub <- pack_stability(samples_Carpathians, rel, "QG", 0.25, fraction = c(0.9, 0.75, 0.5, 0.25), n_sub = 10,
                      reference = reference_Carpathians, period = "Campaign")
sub$subsampling
```

# References

Iosif, R., Skrbinšek, T., Erős, N., Konec, M., Boljte, B., Jan, M., & Promberger-Fürpass, B. (2025). Wolf population size and composition in one of Europe's strongholds, the Romanian Carpathians. Ecology and Evolution, 15(4), e71200. https://doi.org/10.1002/ece3.71200

Kanishka, Koley, S., Khan, S., Hussain, Z., Sathyakumar, S., & Habib, B. (2026). The missing metric in ecological studies: Land tenure system of territorial carnivores. Journal of Animal Ecology. https://doi.org/10.1111/1365-2656.70373
